item.content:encoded:
dax (@thdxr) · post

the focus on whether you read the code or not is the wrong thing to look at


if you have software you're responsible for, you should be able to answer questions from memory about how it works


the expectations for how well you can do this should not be any different now

Kent C. Dodds (@kentcdodds) · context

I was just thinking about this actually. This is difficult to scale compared to times past. I now have a codebase I built solo starting in March that is 500k lines of code. I'm not done evolving it either (lines will be removed as I narrow down primitives, but more lines will be added as I increase features and add/expand primitives).


I feel like I have a pretty good handle on how most things work, but a single dev having the whole system of a codebase like this available in memory feels like something we never would have expected of anyone before.


It's just different now and I do believe you should understand the system-level changes that are being made as the software evolves, but are just able to build such large systems solo now I do think it's different.

dax (@thdxr) · reply

i think it scales how it would before. what do you expect of someone leading a team working on this codebase

client/local agent generates the keypair and gets the cert, the private key never leaves the machine. the relay only forwards raw tcp and tls is terminated by the local agent itself

item.title: Mitchell Hashimoto reply: All http/https is trusted since the preview is visible and browsers have their own security barri...
item.author: Mitchell Hashimoto
item.description: Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post OSC8 is the terminal sequence for linking arbitrary text (similar to `a` tags in HTML). It is mandatory for a modern terminal experience but prone to malicious use. The next version of Ghostty contains the strongest protections for malici...
item.content:encoded:
Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post

OSC8 is the terminal sequence for linking arbitrary text (similar to `a` tags in HTML). It is mandatory for a modern terminal experience but prone to malicious use. The next version of Ghostty contains the strongest protections for malicious OSC8 short of disabling it entirely.


In the next version of Ghostty, we've added a classifier for OSC8 URLs (any hidden URL, really) that classifies a URL as: trusted, requires-confirmation, or deny. The screenshots below show the separate requires-confirmation and deny alerts.


We also now show hidden characters in the URL preview in the bottom of the window (previously we interpreted the Unicode directly which allowed maliciously crafted URLs to hide themselves). Hidden characters immediately trigger the `deny` classification, too.


These are the strongest, most comprehensive protections for OSC8 across terminals. As a comparison:


* Alacritty, Kitty, iTerm2, WezTerm: enabled by default with zero filtering at all. Can directly open executables or maliciously crafted schemes without any filter. Can hide the real URL through Unicode tricks.


* Gnome Terminal: enables all OSC8, no configuration I could find to disable. Only rejects remote-host `file://` URLs. No other sanitization, confirmation, etc.


* VS Code Terminal: Allowlist of safe protocols, prompts for unknown, silently replaces whitespace characters. Very good!


* Windows Terminal: Allowlist, prompts for anything executable, prompts for any custom schemes. Very good!

Olivier Mengué (@omengue) · context

I can't even imagine what URL could be marked as trusted except purely ASCII and exactly the same as the displayed text.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

All http/https is trusted since the preview is visible and browsers have their own security barriers. Local files are trusted if they're non-executable and readable and advertise a text format. etc.

bitwise (@bitwise0x2a) · original

I built Remux, a mobile-first tmux client for iPhone, powered by libghostty.


It uses tmux control mode to bring remote sessions, windows, and panes into a native mobile UI. It's open source and now in beta.


Thanks

@mitchellh

and the Ghostty contributors for making this possible


code:

https://

github.com/h3nock/remux

Rob Pruzan (@robknight__) · context

does it support the kitty graphics protocol?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Tmux itself doesn't so it can't unless they forked it. Ghostty supports unicode placeholders (the only terminal other than Kitty too) so compliant Kitty graphics producing applications can use that and it works.

When it's ready, but hoping within months

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Believe it or not, yes

I am just wondering. Can't you take app icons from .desktop files (on linux, not sure about mac alternative) instead of shipping hundreds of icons yourself?

No Linux app yet, just bandwidth constraint. Depending on hiring and so on would love to get there. We have the vision just need the hours :)

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

I should clarify: the server has no problem and the browser app has no problem and the legacy TUI has no problem. I’m talking about a native app

mac only?

No

@almonk

Hand-drawn, hand-curated, and we'll do that for hundreds of things. We're also experimenting with a new terminal protocol to ship icon sets (that work in a variety of sizes, light/dark, etc.). We're also playing with things like Apple foundation models.

item.content:encoded:
Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post

A sad thing I see is when companies start becoming reactive over proactive. Its a clear external sign that the leadership has lost vision. They make decisions they feel are safe instead of through conviction of a future. The problem is that "safe" almost always means following someone else.


This isn't a clear sign of death, but it is a very difficult position to be in...


For me personally, I hate seeing it because so many companies start with a genuinely interesting vision. Then the world changes, they lose confidence in that vision, and instead of finding a new way to adapt and express it, they start chasing whatever everyone else is doing.


It happens during every major secular shift. AI is the obvious current example. A lot of companies that looked exciting just a few years ago now feel like they're playing catch-up instead of leading. Its a tough thing to watch.

Carl Lerche (@carllerche) · context

I agree, though AI is a huge shift and it is really hard to predict where exactly it is heading. Curious if you have any specific examples you are OK calling out.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

I don't feel comfortable calling anyone out... And yes its hard to predict but thats the whole job of being the "visionary founder." You start with some audacious vision of where the future is going, then it shifts, then you fail to adapt to that shift. It is hard.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

And fwiw, its not a "failure." I shouldn't have used that word. It is genuinely hard, and I feel really bad, and you can't expect people to reliably do this. Its just hard to watch because these people are usually both really smart AND had a compelling vision before and you just wanted the best for them.
